e-3694.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables
e-3694.problem: If $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2 y^3$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \sin t \ \mathbf i + e^{t} \ \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
e-3694.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+6{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t$ and $y=e^{t}$  into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+6({e}^{t})^{2}\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6{e}^{2t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+6{e}^{2t}\text{ }j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }i+{e}^{t}\text{ }j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3695.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables
e-3695.problem: If $f(x,y,z) = xz\ln{y}$ and $\mathbf r (t) =  t^2 \, \mathbf i + t  \, \mathbf j +t^3  \, \mathbf k,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
e-3695.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,i+\frac{xz}{y}\,j+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x= t^2,$ $y = t$ and $z= t^3$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+{t}^{4}\,j+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+{t}^{4}\,j+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{4})\cdot 1+({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 3{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{4}+3{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & ={t}^{4}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

e-8282.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
e-8282.problem:
Evaluate $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}[f(\mathbf r(t))]$ at $t = \pi$ given that
$\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x-1) \, \mathbf j$
and
$\mathbf r (t) = \sin{t} \, \mathbf i + \cos{t} \, \mathbf j.$
e-8282.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x - 1) \, \mathbf j.
$$

First, we substitute $x = \sin{t}$ and $y = \cos{t}$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t = \pi,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(1)+0-(-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3696.knowledge_point: Computing the Rate of Change of a Multivariable Function at a Point Using the Chain Rule
e-3696.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2-z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \left \langle \sin t, \cos t, t  \right \rangle$ at the point $t=\dfrac \pi 4.$
e-3696.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The gradient is ∇f(x,y)=(1/x,2/y). Thus ∇f(r(t))=(t²,2e^(-t)) and r′(t)=(-2t^(-3),e^t). Their dot product is -2/t+2=2(t-1)/t, for t≠0.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$

$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2) and r(t)=t−2i+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
t2et+2et
b
3(t2+1)t
c
2(tet−1)et
d
t(t−2)
e
2(t−1)t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(xy2)i+∂∂yln⁡(xy2)j=y2xy2i+2xyxy2j=1xi+2yj

Next, we substitute x=t−2 and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1t−2i+2etj=t2i+2e−tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(et)j=−2t−3i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(t2i+2e−tj)⋅(−2t−3i+etj)=−2(t2)(t−3)+2e−t(et)=2−2t=2(t−1)t.

verification.explanation: Direct substitution gives f(r(t))=ln(t^(-2)e^(2t))=2t−2ln|t| for t≠0. Differentiating yields 2−2/t=2(t−1)/t, confirming option e and the revealed worked solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitution gives f(r(t))=2ln(t)−9t^4ln(t). Applying the product rule gives 2/t−36t^3ln(t)−9t^3 for t>0, which matches option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2-{y}^{2})\,i-2xy\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=3{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j) \\  & =(2-9{t}^{4})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 6t \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-9{t}^{3}-36{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=2x−xy2 and r(t)=ln⁡ti+3t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t
b
2+9t3+6t3ln⁡t
c
2t−9t2−12t2ln⁡t
d
2t−3t−3tln⁡t
e
2t−3t2+36t3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(2x−xy2)i+∂∂y(2x−xy2)j=(2−y2)i−2xyj

Next, we substitute x=ln⁡t and y=3t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=(2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(3t2)j=1ti+6tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj)⋅(1ti+6tj)=(2−9t4)⋅1t+(−6t2ln⁡t)⋅6t=2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t.

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
 et(sin⁡t+1)1+e2tsin2⁡t
b
et(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)1+e2tsin2⁡t

 et(cos⁡t+1)1+e2tsin2⁡t

 sin⁡t+et1+e2tsin2⁡t

 et−cos⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡t

decision.explanation: Substitution gives f(r(t))=arctan(e^t sin(t)). Using the chain and product rules, its derivative is e^t(sin(t)+cos(t))/(1+e^(2t)sin²(t)), matching option b.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=arctan⁡xy and r(t)=eti+sin⁡tj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 et(sin⁡t+1)1+e2tsin2⁡t
b
et(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)1+e2tsin2⁡t
c
 et(cos⁡t+1)1+e2tsin2⁡t
d
 sin⁡t+et1+e2tsin2⁡t
e
 et−cos⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(arctan⁡xy)i+∂∂y(arctan⁡xy)j=y1+x2y2i+x1+x2y2j 

Next, we substitute x=et and y=sin⁡t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=sin⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡ti+et1+e2tsin2⁡tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(et)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=eti+cos⁡tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡ti+et1+e2tsin2⁡tj)⋅(eti+cos⁡tj)=etsin⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡t+etcos⁡t1+e2tsin2⁡t=et(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)1+e2tsin2⁡t.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\pi t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=ycos⁡x and r(t)=πti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 πt−etsin⁡πt
b
 πt+etcos⁡πt
c
 etcos⁡πt−sin⁡πt
d
et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt)
e
 cos⁡πt−etsin⁡πt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(ycos⁡x)i+∂∂y(ycos⁡x)j=−ysin⁡xi+cos⁡xj

Next, we substitute x=πt and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(πt)i+ddt(et)j=πi+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj)⋅(πi+etj)=−πetsin⁡πt+etcos⁡πt=et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt).

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\pi t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitution gives f(r(t))=sin⁴(t)−cos⁴(t)−cos(2t). Since sin⁴(t)−cos⁴(t)=−cos(2t), this equals −2cos(2t). Its derivative is 4sin(2t), matching option d.

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,k \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$

$$

Question 6
?

If f(x,y,z)=x4−y4−cos⁡z and r(t)=sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj+2tk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
sin⁡2tcos3⁡2t
b
cos2⁡t
c
0
d
4sin⁡2t
e
cos⁡tsin3⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z): ∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(x4−y4−cos⁡z)i+∂∂y(x4−y4−cos⁡z)j+∂∂z(x4−y4−cos⁡z)k=4x3i−4y3j+sin⁡zk

Next, we substitute x=sin⁡t, y=cos⁡t and z=2t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=4sin3⁡ti−4cos3⁡tj+sin⁡2tk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(2t)k=cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+2k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(4sin3⁡ti−4cos3⁡tj+sin⁡2tk)⋅(cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+2k)=4sin3⁡t⋅cos⁡t−4cos3⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+sin⁡2t⋅2=4sin3⁡tcos⁡t+4cos3⁡tsin⁡t+2sin⁡2t=4sin⁡tcos⁡t(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)+2sin⁡2t=4sin⁡tcos⁡t+2sin⁡2t=2sin⁡2t+2sin⁡2t=4sin⁡2t.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,k \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\,k) \\  & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}[x({y}^{2}-{z}^{2})]\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}[x({y}^{2}-{z}^{2})]\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}[x({y}^{2}-{z}^{2})]\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,i+2xy\,j-2xz\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,$ $y=t+1$ and $z=t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =[(t+1)^{2}-(t-1)^{2}]i+2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot (t+1)\,j-2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot (t-1)\,k \\  & =4t\,i+2(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j-2(t-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+\,j+\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4t\,i+2(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j-2(t-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+\,j+\,k) \\  & =4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot 1-2(t-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot 1 \\  & =4+2(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t-2(t-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & =4+4\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x[x(y2−z2)]i+∂∂y[x(y2−z2)]j+∂∂z[x(y2−z2)]k=(y2−z2)i+2xyj−2xzk

Next, we substitute x=ln⁡t, y=t+1 and z=t−1 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=[(t+1)2−(t−1)2]i+2ln⁡t⋅(t+1)j−2ln⁡t⋅(t−1)k=4ti+2(t+1)ln⁡tj−2(t−1)ln⁡tk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(t+1)j+ddt(t−1)k=1ti+j+k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(4ti+2(t+1)ln⁡tj−2(t−1)ln⁡tk)⋅(1ti+j+k)=4t⋅1t+2(t+1)ln⁡t⋅1−2(t−1)ln⁡t⋅1=4+2(t+1)ln⁡t−2(t−1)ln⁡t=4+4ln⁡t=4(ln⁡t+1).

Question 8

If f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz) and r(t)=ti+et−1j+etk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 3
b
2t+1t
c
 et+1t
d
 2et−1(1−t)
e
2tet+1t
Submit

decision.explanation: Substitution gives f(r(t))=ln(te^(2t−1))=ln(t)+2t−1 for t>0. Differentiating yields 1/t+2=(2t+1)/t, matching option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =\frac{yz}{xyz}\,i+\frac{xz}{xyz}\,j+\frac{xy}{xyz}\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j+\frac{1}{z}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t-1},$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t-1}}\,j+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t-1}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t-1}}\,j+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t-1}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{t}+\frac{{e}^{t-1}}{{e}^{t-1}}+\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}+2 \\  & =\frac{2t+1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

If f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz) and r(t)=ti+et−1j+etk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 3
b
2t+1t
c
 et+1t
d
 2et−1(1−t)
e
2tet+1t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z): ∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))j+∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))k=yzxyzi+xzxyzj+xyxyzk=1xi+1yj+1zk

Next, we substitute x=t,y=et−1, and z=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1ti+1et−1j+1etk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et−1)j+ddt(et)k=i+et−1j+etk.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(1ti+1et−1j+1etk)⋅(i+et−1j+etk)=1t+et−1et−1+etet=1t+2=2t+1t.

Question 9
?

If f(x,y,z)=yzcos⁡x and r(t)=t2i+etj+etk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2e2t
b
e2tcos⁡t
c
e2t(2cos⁡t2−sin⁡t2)
d
e2t(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)
e
2e2t(cos⁡t2−tsin⁡t2)
Submit

decision.explanation: Substitution gives f(r(t))=e^(2t)cos(t²). The product and chain rules yield 2e^(2t)cos(t²)−2te^(2t)sin(t²)=2e^(2t)(cos(t²)−t sin(t²)), matching option e.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,k \\  & =-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+z\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y={e}^{t},$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}-t\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y,z)=yzcos⁡x and r(t)=t2i+etj+etk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

e2tcos⁡t

e

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(yzcos⁡x)i+∂∂y(yzcos⁡x)j+∂∂z(yzcos⁡x)k=−yzsin⁡xi+zcos⁡xj+ycos⁡xk

Next, we substitute x=t2,y=et, and z=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=−e2tsin⁡t2i+etcos⁡t2j+etcos⁡t2k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(et)j+ddt(et)k=2ti+etj+etk.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−e2tsin⁡t2i+etcos⁡t2j+etcos⁡t2k)⋅(2ti+etj+etk)=−2te2tsin⁡t2+etcos⁡t2⋅et+etcos⁡t2⋅et=−2te2tsin⁡t2+2e2tcos⁡t2=2e2t(cos⁡t2−tsin⁡t2).

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,k \\  & =-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+z\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y={e}^{t},$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}-t\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{t}^{2}}\,j+t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xz)+ey and r(t)=sin⁡ti+t2j+1tk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
tan⁡t+et2t2
b
csc⁡t+2tet2
c
cot⁡t+et2−1
d
csc⁡t+et2+t
e
cot⁡t+2tet2−1t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(ln⁡(xz)+ey)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xz)+ey)j+∂∂z(ln⁡(xz)+ey)k=1xi+eyj+1zk

Next, we substitute x=sin⁡t,y=t2, and z=1t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1sin⁡ti+et2j+tk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(t2)j+ddt(1t)k=cos⁡ti+2tj−1t2k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(1sin⁡ti+et2j+tk)⋅(cos⁡ti+2tj−1t2k)=cos⁡tsin⁡t+2tet2−tt2=cot⁡t+2tet2−1t.

content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+{e}^{y}\,j+\frac{1}{z}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,y={t}^{2},$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{t}^{2}}\,j+t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{t}^{2}}\,j+t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\,i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={e}^{2t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}+1)\,i+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(2t+1)\,i+2t{e}^{2t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(2t+1)\,i+2t{e}^{2t}\,j)\cdot (2{e}^{2t}\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(2t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+4t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}[(2t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=0,$ we obtain

content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\,i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={e}^{2t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}+1)\,i+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(2t+1)\,i+2t{e}^{2t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)(2t+1)\,i+2t{e}^{2t}\,j)\cdot (2{e}^{2t}\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(2t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+4t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}[(2t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=0,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =2{e}^{2(0)}((2(0)+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))+2(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0)))=0.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\frac{t}{2}$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{2}))] & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=sin⁡yi+xcos⁡yj.

First, we substitute x=t2 and y=t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=sin⁡ti+t2cos⁡tj.

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(t)j=12i+j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡ti+t2cos⁡tj)⋅(12i+j)=sin⁡t⋅12+t2cos⁡t⋅1=12(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t).

Finally, evaluating the above at t=π2, we obtain ddt[f(r(π2))]=12(sin⁡(π2)+π2cos⁡(π2))=12(1+π2⋅0)=12.

verification.explanation: The chain rule gives (sin(t), (t/2)cos(t))·(1/2,1)=(sin(t)+t cos(t))/2. At t=π/2, this is 1/2, confirming option e and the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option c.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,i-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=-2\sqrt{t}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-(-2\sqrt{t})\operatorname{sin}⁡[(2\sqrt{t})(-2\sqrt{t})]\,i-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡[(2\sqrt{t})(-2\sqrt{t})]\,j \\  & =-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\sqrt{t})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})i) \\  & =(-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{8}))] & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=−ysin⁡(xy)i−xsin⁡(xy)j.

First, we substitute x=2t and y=−2t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=−(−2t)sin⁡[(2t)(−2t)]i−2tsin⁡[(2t)(−2t)]j=−2tsin⁡(4t)i+2tsin⁡(4t)j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(2t)i+ddt(−2t)j=1ti+(−1t)j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−2tsin⁡(4t)i+2tsin⁡(4t)j)⋅(1ti+(−1t)i)=(−2tsin⁡(4t))⋅1t+2tsin⁡(4t)⋅(−1t)=−2sin⁡(4t)−2sin⁡(4t)=−4sin⁡(4t).

Finally, evaluating the above at t=π8, we obtain ddt[f(r(π8))]=−4sin⁡(4⋅π8)=−4sin⁡(π2)=−4.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,i-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=-2\sqrt{t}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-(-2\sqrt{t})\operatorname{sin}⁡[(2\sqrt{t})(-2\sqrt{t})]\,i-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡[(2\sqrt{t})(-2\sqrt{t})]\,j \\  & =-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\sqrt{t})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})i) \\  & =(-2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+2\sqrt{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{8}))] & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t}⟩$ at the point $t=9.$
after.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the rate of change of the function f(x,y)=xy with respect to t along the curve r(t)=⟨2t,t⟩ at the point t=9.

a
1
b
−3
c
13
d
−19
e
13
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The rate of change of f(x,y) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(xy),∂∂y(xy)⟩=⟨1y,−xy2⟩

Next, we substitute x=2t and y=t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=⟨1t,−2⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=⟨ddt(2t),ddt(t)⟩=⟨2,12t⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨1t,−2⟩⋅⟨2,12t⟩=1t⋅2−2⋅12t=2t−1t=1t.

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=9 is ddt[f(r(9))]=19=13.

verification.explanation: Direct substitution gives f(r(t))=2√t, whose derivative is 1/√t. At t=9 this equals 1/3, confirming option e and the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option d.

content.knowledge_point: Computing the Rate of Change of a Multivariable Function at a Point Using the Chain Rule
content.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t}⟩$ at the point $t=9.$
content.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},3{y}^{2},2xz⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=4$ and $z=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3})^{2},3(4)^{2},2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩ \\  & =({t}^{2}-3)\cdot 1+48\cdot 0+2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}} \\  & ={t}^{2}-3+0+2{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =3(2)^{2}-3 \\  & =12-3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=2 is ddt[f(r(2))]=3(2)2−3=12−3=9.

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},3{y}^{2},2xz⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=4$ and $z=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3})^{2},3(4)^{2},2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩ \\  & =({t}^{2}-3)\cdot 1+48\cdot 0+2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}} \\  & ={t}^{2}-3+0+2{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =3(2)^{2}-3 \\  & =12-3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

The rate of change of f(x,y,z) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(xz2+y3),∂∂y(xz2+y3),∂∂z(xz2+y3)⟩=⟨z2,3y2,2xz⟩

Next, we substitute x=t, y=4 and z=t2−3 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=⟨(t2−3)2,3(4)2,2tt2−3⟩=⟨t2−3,48,2tt2−3⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=⟨ddt(t),ddt(4),t2−3⟩=⟨1,0,tt2−3⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨t2−3,48,2tt2−3⟩⋅⟨1,0,tt2−3⟩=(t2−3)⋅1+48⋅0+2tt2−3⋅tt2−3=t2−3+0+2t2=3t2−3.

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=2 is ddt[f(r(2))]=3(2)2−3=12−3=9.

after.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{x}^{2},2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}-4}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{x}^{2},2y⟩\end{aligned}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$

after.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t-1,3,2t⟩$ at the point $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\  & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\  & =\frac{-2}{10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
